content: 1. Arrhythmias may occur as a result of certain drug interactions or conditions. 2. Magnesium hydroxide can reduce the plasma levels or efficacy of raltegravir by binding to it in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. This interaction necessitates avoiding or using alternative medications. Magnesium-containing antacids should not be taken within 6 hours of raltegravir administration. Close monitoring is recommended. 3. Calcium carbonate decreases the effectiveness of ramipril through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 4. Calcium carbonate reduces the levels or effects of rifampin by interfering with its absorption in the GI tract. Antacids may reduce rifampin absorption, so rifampin should be administered at least 1 hour before antacids. Close monitoring is required. 5. Calcium carbonate decreases rilpivirine levels by increasing gastric pH, which applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration of antacids with rilpivirine can significantly reduce rilpivirine plasma concentrations. Antacids should be taken at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after rilpivirine. For the combination product dolutegravir/rilpivirine, antacids should be taken at least 4 hours before or 6 hours after administration. Close monitoring is advised. 6. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the levels of riociguat by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 7. Calcium carbonate decreases riociguat levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by at least 1 hour. Close monitoring is recommended. 8. Calcium carbonate reduces risedronate levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 30 minutes. Close monitoring is required. 9. Calcium carbonate decreases the levels or effects of rose hips by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Rose hips may increase calcium carbonate levels by enhancing GI absorption. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown, but close monitoring is advised. 10. Calcium carbonate reduces rosuvastatin levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 2 hours. Close monitoring is recommended. 11. Calcium carbonate interacts with salicylates (non-ASA) through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH. Salicylate levels may increase at moderate doses and decrease at large doses due to increased renal excretion of unchanged salicylic acid. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 12. Calcium carbonate interacts with salsalate through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH. Salicylate levels may increase at moderate doses and decrease at large doses due to increased renal excretion of unchanged salicylic acid. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 13. Magnesium hydroxide reduces sarecycline levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Multivalent cation-containing products may impair tetracycline absorption, reducing its efficacy. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 14. Calcium carbonate reduces sarecycline levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. Dosing of tetracyclines should be separated from these products. 15. Calcium carbonate interacts with shark cartilage through pharmacodynamic synergism, potentially leading to hypercalcemia. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, but close monitoring is advised. 16. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of sodium phosphates (IV) by cation binding in the GI tract. Calcium decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 17. Magnesium hydroxide reduces the effects of sodium phosphates (IV) by cation binding in the GI tract. Magnesium decreases serum phosphate concentrations by binding dietary phosphate. Alternatives should be used if available. 18. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate increases magnesium hydroxide levels by decreasing renal clearance. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate also increases calcium carbonate levels by decreasing renal clearance. These interactions may increase the risk of alkalosis. The clinical significance is unknown. 19. Magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride increases the toxicity of calcium carbonate. Co-administration with medications causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Close monitoring is required. 20. Sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate increases the toxicity of calcium carbonate. Co-administration with medications causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Close monitoring is required. 21. Calcium carbonate reduces the levels or effects of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir by increasing gastric pH. Velpatasvir solubility decreases as gastric pH increases, becoming practically insoluble at pH >5. Administration of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir should be separated from antacids by at least 4 hours. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 22. Calcium carbonate reduces sotalol levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 2 hours. Close monitoring is recommended. 23. Magnesium hydroxide reduces sotorasib levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent cannot be avoided, sotorasib should be administered 4 hours before or 10 hours after a locally-acting antacid. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 24. Calcium carbonate reduces sotorasib levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. If co-administration with an acid-reducing agent cannot be avoided, sotorasib should be administered 4 hours before or 10 hours after a locally-acting antacid. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 25. Calcium carbonate reduces sparsentan levels by increasing gastric pH. Antacids may decrease sparsentan exposure, potentially reducing its efficacy. Sparsentan should be administered 2 hours before or after antacids. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 26. Spironolactone decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. Spironolactone increases magnesium hydroxide levels by decreasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 27. Calcium carbonate increases the toxicity of squill through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 28. Streptomycin decreases calcium carbonate levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. Streptomycin also decreases magnesium hydroxide levels by increasing renal clearance. These interactions apply only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 29. Calcium carbonate reduces strontium ranelate levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 2 hours. Close monitoring is recommended. 30. Calcium carbonate interacts with sulfasalazine through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH. Salicylate levels may increase at moderate doses and decrease at large doses due to increased renal excretion of unchanged salicylic acid. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 31. Teriparatide increases calcium carbonate levels through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 32. Magnesium hydroxide reduces tetracycline levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 33. Calcium carbonate and tetracycline can each reduce the levels of the other by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 2 hours. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 34. Calcium carbonate reduces tiludronate levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 30 minutes. Close monitoring is required. 35. Calcium carbonate reduces timolol levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 2 hours. Close monitoring is recommended. 36. Tobramycin decreases magnesium hydroxide levels by increasing renal clearance. Tobramycin also decreases calcium carbonate levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. These interactions apply only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance is unknown. 37. Torsemide decreases magnesium hydroxide levels by increasing renal clearance. Torsemide also decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 38. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of trandolapril through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 39. Triamcinolone acetonide injectable suspension decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing elimination. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 40. Triamterene increases magnesium hydroxide levels by decreasing renal clearance. Triamterene also decreases calcium carbonate levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 41. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 42. Calcium carbonate reduces vadadustat levels by drug binding in the GI tract. Vadadustat should be administered at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after dosing non-iron-containing phosphate binders. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 43. Calcium carbonate reduces the effects of verapamil through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. 44. Magnesium hydroxide reduces vismodegib levels by altering its solubility due to increased gastric pH, which reduces bioavailability. The effect on efficacy is unknown. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 45. Calcium carbonate reduces vismodegib levels by altering its solubility due to increased gastric pH, which reduces bioavailability. The effect on efficacy is unknown. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 46. Vitamin D increases magnesium hydroxide levels by increasing serum magnesium concentrations, particularly in the presence of renal impairment. The combined use of vitamin D and magnesium-containing products should be avoided in patients with chronic renal failure. Therapy modification or close monitoring is required. 47. Calcium carbonate interacts with willow bark through passive renal tubular reabsorption due to increased pH. Salicylate levels may increase at moderate doses and decrease at large doses due to increased renal excretion of unchanged salicylic acid. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 48. Calcium carbonate reduces zoledronic acid levels by inhibiting its GI absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Administration should be separated by 30 minutes. Close monitoring is required. 49. Magnesium hydroxide should be used with caution in patients with neuromuscular diseases (e.g., myasthenia gravis) and renal insufficiency. 50. Calcium carbonate should be used with caution in patients with a history of kidney stones, as it may increase the risk of recurrence. 51. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk, making these medications generally acceptable during pregnancy.
